title: Venus venatrix. Dido et Pygmalion
titleEn: The Huntress in the Wood — Aeneid I.297–386
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Jupiter's messenger, Mercury, flies down to Libya and softens Dido's heart toward the Trojans. Next morning Aeneas hides his fleet in a wooded inlet and sets out to scout the unknown coast with one companion, Achates. In the forest his mother Venus meets him disguised as a Spartan-style huntress, and asks whether they have seen her sisters hunting; Aeneas, sensing a goddess, greets her as one and asks where on earth they have landed. She answers with the history of Carthage: Dido, a Tyrian princess, whose husband Sychaeus was secretly murdered at the altar by her brother Pygmalion for his gold; his ghost appeared to her in a dream, showed her the wound, and told her where treasure lay hidden; she fled with a band of followers, and bought a plot of ground, the Byrsa, as large as an ox-hide would cover. Then she asks who the strangers are, and Aeneas begins his answer, naming himself and his search for Italy, before Venus cuts him short.

sentences.t:
Haec ait, et Maia genitum demittit ab alto,
ut terrae, utque novae pateant Karthaginis arces
hospitio Teucris, ne fati nescia Dido
finibus arceret:
sentences.l:
These things he says, and Maia's son he sends down from on high,
that the lands and the new citadels of Karthago may lie open
for welcome to the Teucrians, lest Dido, ignorant of fate,
should keep them from her borders:
sentences.i: So he speaks, and sends Maia's son down from the heights, so that the land and the towers of the new Karthago may stand open in welcome to the Trojans, and Dido, not knowing what fate intends, may not bar them from her borders:
sentences.n: 'Haec ait' — the speech of Jupiter (I.257–296, in aeneid-003) is over. 'Maia genitum' — 'the one born of Maia', Mercury (Greek Hermes), the gods' messenger; 'genitum' is a perfect participle used as a noun, and 'Maia' is an ablative of origin (no preposition needed). 'demittit' — historic present. 'ut… pateant' and 'ne… arceret' — two purpose clauses, the first with the present subjunctive and the second with the imperfect. 'novae Karthaginis' — Greenough prints 'Karthago', not 'Carthago'; the town is still new. 'hospitio' — dative of purpose, 'for hospitality'. 'Teucris' — dative, 'Teucrians' = Trojans (from their ancestor Teucer). 'fati nescia' — 'ignorant of fate': 'nescius' takes the genitive; Dido does not know that the gods have a destiny for Aeneas. 'finibus arceret' — 'keep (them) away from her borders' (ablative of separation).

sentences.t:
volat ille per aera magnum
remigio alarum, ac Libyae citus adstitit oris.
sentences.l:
he flies, he, through the great air
by the oarage of his wings, and swiftly stood at Libya's shores.
sentences.i: he flies through the wide air, rowing with his wings, and quickly alights on the Libyan coast.
sentences.n: 'remigio alarum' — 'by the oar-work of his wings': a bird's wings as oars, a metaphor that Virgil likes (compare 'remigium alarum' again at VI.19). 'aera' is a Greek accusative singular ('aer, aeris'). 'Libyae… oris' — 'Libya' to Virgil is North Africa, and 'orae' are coasts. 'adstitit' — perfect of 'adsto', 'stood by, alighted', after the vivid present 'volat'.

sentences.t:
Et iam iussa facit, ponuntque ferocia Poeni
corda volente deo;
sentences.l:
And now he does the bidden things, and lay aside their fierce
hearts the Phoenicians, the god willing;
sentences.i: And now he carries out the orders: the Carthaginians put aside their fierce hearts, since the god wills it;
sentences.n: 'iussa facit' — 'does the things ordered' ('iussa' is the neuter plural perfect participle of 'iubeo' used as a noun). 'Poeni' — the Phoenicians (the Latin 'Poenus' gives us 'Punic'): the Carthaginians were Phoenician settlers from Tyre. 'volente deo' — ablative absolute, 'the god willing'. Here 'deo' is Mercury, though a reader will sense Jupiter behind him. 'ponunt' — 'lay down', the usual verb for putting off an emotion.

sentences.t:
in primis regina quietum
accipit in Teucros animum mentemque benignam.
sentences.l:
in the first place the queen receives a quiet spirit
toward the Teucrians and a kindly mind.
sentences.i: above all the queen takes up a calm temper and a kindly mind toward the Trojans.
sentences.n: 'in primis' — 'in the first place, above all': the queen's change of heart is more complete than that of her people. 'in Teucros' — 'toward' with the accusative. 'quietum… animum mentemque benignam' — 'quietum' is held apart from its noun 'animum' by the verb and 'in Teucros', and 'benignam' goes with 'mentem': a quiet spirit, a kind mind. 'Accipit' continues the idea 'ponunt': a god's will works as a change of mood, not a command.

sentences.t:
At pius Aeneas, per noctem plurima volvens,
ut primum lux alma data est, exire locosque
explorare novos, quas vento accesserit oras,
qui teneant, nam inculta videt, hominesne feraene,
sentences.l:
But dutiful Aeneas, through the night turning over very many things,
as soon as the kindly light was given, to go out and the places
new to explore, to what shores by wind he has come,
who hold them, for uncultivated he sees them, men or wild beasts,
sentences.i: But devoted Aeneas, who has turned over many a plan through the night, resolves, as soon as kindly daylight is given, to go out and explore the unfamiliar country, to find what coast the wind has brought him to, who holds it, for it looks untilled—men or wild beasts—
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a very long sentence that runs on to line 312. 'pius' — Aeneas's standing epithet: loyal in duty to gods, family and people. 'plurima volvens' — 'turning over very many things in his mind'. The main verb is 'constituit' (309); between lie the infinitives it governs, 'exire', 'explorare', 'quaerere'. 'quas… oras' and 'qui teneant' — indirect questions, with 'accesserit' (perfect subjunctive: the arrival is already past) and 'teneant'. 'nam inculta videt' — a parenthesis, 'for he sees the land untilled'. 'hominesne feraene' — 'men or beasts?': '-ne… -ne' in a double question. The unit ends on a comma: the sentence, 305–312, is eight lines, over the five-line limit, so it is cut at 'feraene,' and the main verb opens the next unit (the English 'resolves' anticipates it).

sentences.t:
quaerere constituit, sociisque exacta referre
Classem in convexo nemorum sub rupe cavata
arboribus clausam circum atque horrentibus umbris
occulit;
sentences.l:
to ask, he resolved, and to bring back to his comrades the things found out.
His fleet in the hollow of the groves under a hollowed rock,
shut in all round with trees and with bristling shadows,
he hides;
sentences.i: to ask—such is his resolve—and to carry the findings back to his companions. His fleet he hides under a hollowed cliff in a bend of the woods, shut in on all sides by trees and bristling shade;
sentences.n: 'quaerere constituit' — 'he decided to ask': 'constituo' takes an infinitive. Greenough's text prints no stop after 'referre' (the edition simply runs on): the sentence, from 305, is one long run. 'sociisque exacta referre' — 'and to report the things ascertained to his comrades' ('exacta', neuter plural participle, 'things worked out'). The word order of 310–311 is Virgilian: 'Classem' stands first and far from its verb 'occulit' (312). 'in convexo nemorum' — 'in the curve (hollow) of the woods'. 'rupe cavata' — 'under a hollowed rock'. 'arboribus… horrentibus umbris' — ablatives, 'with trees and with bristling (shuddering) shades' — a dense wood. 'circum atque' — 'circum' is an adverb, 'all round'.

sentences.t:
ipse uno graditur comitatus Achate,
bina manu lato crispans hastilia ferro.
sentences.l:
himself he goes, accompanied by one, Achates,
two spears in hand brandishing with broad iron.
sentences.i: he himself goes forward with only Achates for company, shaking two broad-headed spears in his hand.
sentences.n: 'ipse' — 'he himself', in contrast to the fleet. 'uno… Achate' — ablative with 'comitatus' (the perfect participle of the deponent 'comitor', with active sense, 'accompanied by'); 'uno' is 'one, only one': he takes nobody but Achates. Achates is Aeneas's constant, nearly silent companion, already 'fidus Achates' at I.188. 'bina… hastilia' — 'two spears' ('bini', usually 'two each', is used by poets for a simple pair). 'lato… ferro' — ablative of quality, 'with broad iron (heads)'. 'manu' — 'in hand'. 'crispans' — 'shaking, making them quiver', as a man poises a spear.

sentences.t:
Cui mater media sese tulit obvia silva,
virginis os habitumque gerens, et virginis arma
Spartanae, vel qualis equos Threissa fatigat
Harpalyce, volucremque fuga praevertitur Hebrum.
sentences.l:
To him his mother in the middle of the wood came, in his path,
a virgin's face and bearing wearing, and a virgin's arms
Spartan, or such as the Thracian Harpalyce tires her horses
and outruns in flight the swift Hebrus.
sentences.i: His mother met him in the middle of the wood, wearing a maiden's face and bearing and a Spartan girl's gear—like the Thracian Harpalyce when she tires out her horses and outstrips the swift Hebrus in flight.
sentences.n: Another paragraph. The mother is Venus, though Virgil does not name her until 325. 'sese tulit obvia' — 'carried herself to meet (him)', i.e. appeared in his path; 'obvia' is the adjective 'in the way'. 'media silva' — 'in the middle of the wood' (ablative of place). 'virginis os habitumque gerens' — 'os' is face (here the whole look), 'habitus' bearing and dress. 'virginis arma Spartanae' — 'arma' means her hunting gear; Spartan girls were known as huntresses. 'vel qualis… Harpalyce' — 'or like Harpalyce', a Thracian princess, a legendary runner who outran horses; she is a story from outside the poem, and 'Threissa' is Greenough's spelling of the adjective 'Thracian'. 'praevertitur' — a deponent in the passive form, 'outstrips'. 'Hebrum' — the Hebrus river of Thrace, and the name is the object: she is faster than the river.

sentences.t:
Namque umeris de more habilem suspenderat arcum
venatrix, dederatque comam diffundere ventis,
nuda genu, nodoque sinus collecta fluentis.
sentences.l:
For from her shoulders, as the custom is, a handy bow she had hung,
the huntress, and had let her hair spread out to the winds,
bare as to the knee, and the folds of her garment gathered up in a knot, flowing.
sentences.i: For, as the custom is, she carried a handy bow slung from her shoulders and had given her hair to the winds to scatter, bare to the knee, the loose folds of her gown gathered in a knot.
sentences.n: 'Namque' — 'for', explaining the disguise. 'de more' — 'according to custom'. 'habilem' — 'handy, easy to manage'. 'suspenderat' — pluperfect: the huntress had slung (hung) the bow from her shoulders; and 'dederat comam diffundere' — 'had let her hair spread out' (a poetic infinitive of purpose after 'dare'). 'nuda genu' — 'bare as to the knee': the 'accusative of respect' with an adjective, common in Virgil with words for parts of the body ('os', 'umeros', 'genu'). 'nodo sinus collecta fluentis' — the participle 'collecta' (feminine nominative, agreeing with 'venatrix') is passive in form but middle in sense: 'having gathered (her) flowing folds with a knot'; 'sinus' is an accusative plural and 'fluentis' is Greenough's -is for -es.

sentences.t:
Ac prior, “Heus inquit iuvenes, monstrate mearum
vidistis si quam hic errantem forte sororum,
succinctam pharetra et maculosae tegmine lyncis,
aut spumantis apri cursum clamore prementem.”
sentences.l:
And first, “Ho, says she, young men, show, of my
you have seen, if any, here wandering, by chance, of sisters,
girt up with quiver and in the covering of a spotted lynx,
or a foaming boar's course with shout pressing.”
sentences.i: She speaks first: “You there, young men—tell me whether you have seen one of my sisters wandering here, girt with a quiver and wrapped in the hide of a spotted lynx, or pressing a foaming boar's trail with her cries.”
sentences.n: 'Ac prior' — 'and first (she spoke)': she speaks before they can; the verb 'inquit', 'she says', is dropped into the middle of the speech, which is common in Latin ('Heus inquit iuvenes'). 'Heus' — an attention-getter, 'ho there!' 'monstrate… si… vidistis' — 'show (me)', then 'si' meaning 'whether'. 'quam… sororum' — 'any one of my sisters' (the partitive genitive; 'quam' is indefinite after 'si'). 'errantem', 'succinctam' and 'prementem' — accusative participles agreeing with 'quam' (the missing sister): she is 'wandering', 'girt up (succinctam) with a quiver and in the skin of a lynx', or 'pressing hard on the course of a boar'. 'maculosae tegmine lyncis' — 'tegmen' is a covering, here a pelt. 'clamore' — ablative, 'with a shout', as hunters do.

sentences.t: Sic Venus; et Veneris contra sic filius orsus:
sentences.l: So Venus; and of Venus, in answer, so the son began:
sentences.i: So Venus spoke; and Venus's son, answering her, began in this way:
sentences.n: 'Sic Venus' — the verb of speaking is omitted (you'll see this constantly: 'Sic Venus', 'Haec ait'). 'Veneris… filius' — 'Venus's son', Aeneas; and the reader, who has just been told it is Venus, knows what Aeneas does not. 'orsus' — the perfect participle of the deponent 'ordior' ('to begin'), used with 'est' dropped: 'began (to speak)'. 'contra' — an adverb here, 'in reply'. The formula 'Sic… sic' sets each speaker against the other.

sentences.t: “Nulla tuarum audita mihi neque visa sororum—
sentences.l: “None of your sisters heard by me or seen—
sentences.i: “Not one of your sisters have I heard or seen—
sentences.n: Aeneas's speech begins, and he breaks off at once, with the first of three dashes: Virgil is giving Aeneas a speech that stops and starts as he looks at her. 'Nulla tuarum… sororum' — 'none of your sisters', with 'tuarum' (genitive plural, partitive) separated from 'sororum' by the participles. 'audita mihi neque visa' — 'heard by me and not seen': 'mihi' is the dative of the agent, normal with a perfect participle. 'est' is dropped, so the clause is an exclamation more than a sentence.

sentences.t: O quam te memorem, virgo?
sentences.l: O how you shall I call, maiden?
sentences.i: But what am I to call you, maiden?
sentences.n: 'O quam te memorem, virgo?' — 'O how (by what name) am I to speak of you?'; 'memorem' is a deliberative subjunctive, a question the speaker asks himself. 'quam' is an adverb, 'how?' He does not know whether he is speaking to a woman or a goddess.

sentences.t:
Namque haud tibi voltus
mortalis, nec vox hominem sonat: O, dea certe—
sentences.l:
For not at all to you the face
of a mortal, nor does your voice sound human: O, a goddess surely—
sentences.i: Your face is not a mortal's, and your voice does not ring like a human voice: ah, a goddess for certain—
sentences.n: 'Namque haud tibi voltus mortalis' — 'tibi' is a dative of possession ('to you (there is) a face…'), with 'est' dropped; 'voltus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vultus'. 'nec vox hominem sonat' — 'your voice does not sound of a man' ('hominem' is an internal accusative, 'sound man, smack of man'). 'O, dea certe' — 'O, a goddess surely': he breaks off to guess, with no verb, and then the next unit gives two more guesses ('an Phoebi soror?'). Here Virgil is echoing a famous Homeric meeting, Odysseus and Nausicaa in Odyssey 6, where he asks the same question of the princess: is she a goddess or a mortal?

sentences.t: an Phoebi soror? an nympharum sanguinis una?—
sentences.l: or Phoebus' sister? or of the nymphs' blood one?—
sentences.i: or Apollo's sister? or one of the nymphs' kin?—
sentences.n: 'Phoebi soror' — Phoebus is Apollo; his sister is Diana, goddess of the hunt, the obvious guess for a huntress. 'nympharum sanguinis una' — 'one of the nymphs' blood', i.e. 'one born of the nymphs', 'sanguinis' as a genitive of origin. The question is parenthetical, closed by the dash; the sentence resumes with the subjunctives in 330.

sentences.t:
sis felix, nostrumque leves, quaecumque, laborem,
et, quo sub caelo tandem, quibus orbis in oris
iactemur, doceas.
sentences.l:
may you be kind, and lighten our toil, whoever you are,
and under what sky, in what shores of the world
we are tossed, may you teach.
sentences.i: be kind to us, whoever you are, and ease our hardship, and teach us under what sky and on what edge of the world we are being driven about.
sentences.n: 'sis felix' — 'may you be fortunate, kind (to us)': a wish, with the present subjunctive. 'leves' — 'may you lighten', second person singular present subjunctive of 'levo' (so it is a second wish). 'quaecumque' — 'whoever (you are)': feminine nominative singular, 'quaecumque (es)', because she is a woman or goddess; the hedge is the sort the Romans used in prayer when unsure of a god's name or identity. 'doceas' — another wish: 'may you teach'. 'quo sub caelo… quibus orbis in oris' — indirect question, 'under what sky, on what shores of the world': in both phrases the preposition stands inside its phrase ('sub quo caelo' becomes 'quo sub caelo', 'in quibus oris' becomes 'quibus… in oris'), and 'orbis' is a genitive, 'of the (round) world'. 'iactemur' — 'we are tossed about', present passive subjunctive in the indirect question.

sentences.t:
Ignari hominumque locorumque
erramus, vento huc vastis et fluctibus acti:
sentences.l:
Ignorant both of men and of places
we wander, by wind here and by vast waves driven:
sentences.i: We are strangers to the people and the places; we roam, driven here by wind and huge waves:
sentences.n: 'Ignari hominumque locorumque' — 'ignarus' takes the genitive (as 'nescia' at line 299). The double '-que… -que' ties the two genitives. The -que of 'locorumque' is elided into the first word of the next line, 'erramus', so line 332 has a syllable too many for its own measure (a hypermetric line). 'vento… et fluctibus' — ablative of means. 'acti' — nominative plural masculine perfect participle of 'ago': 'driven'. 'huc' — 'to this place'. The colon sets up the promise that follows, which is the promise of a sacrifice.

sentences.t: multa tibi ante aras nostra cadet hostia dextra.”
sentences.l: many a victim before your altars shall fall by our right hand.”
sentences.i: Many a victim will fall before your altars, struck by our right hand.”
sentences.n: A vow, in the future tense. 'multa… hostia' — 'hostia' is the sacrificial victim; 'multa' is singular, 'many a victim' ('multa… hostia cadet'). 'ante aras' — 'before your altars'. 'nostra… dextra' — 'by our right hand': 'nostra' and 'dextra' are both singular ablatives, so 'our' is plural but the hand is one, a collective right hand that does the sacrificing, all of them acting as one. 'cadet' is the usual verb for a victim that 'falls' under the knife. The speech closes with this unit.

sentences.t: Tum Venus: “Haud equidem tali me dignor honore;
sentences.l: Then Venus: “Not indeed of such an honour do I deem myself worthy;
sentences.i: Then Venus: “I do not, in truth, think myself worthy of such an honour;
sentences.n: A new paragraph; Venus answers him in a speech that runs to 370, the longest of the part. She is speaking in the character of a Tyrian girl, and the speech tells the story of Dido. 'Tum Venus' — 'then Venus' (verb of speaking dropped). 'Haud equidem' — 'not indeed I': 'equidem' is an emphatic 'I for my part', mostly with the first person. 'dignor' — a deponent, 'I deem worthy', here with the ablative 'honore': 'I do not consider myself worthy of such an honour'. The refusal is true and false at once: she is a goddess, but she will not say so.

sentences.t:
virginibus Tyriis mos est gestare pharetram,
purpureoque alte suras vincire cothurno.
sentences.l:
for Tyrian maidens it is the custom to carry the quiver,
and with purple, high up, the calves to bind with buskin.
sentences.i: it is the Tyrian girls' custom to carry the quiver and to bind their calves, high up, in purple buskins.
sentences.n: 'virginibus Tyriis mos est' — dative of possession again, 'to Tyrian girls there is a custom'; 'mos est… gestare… vincire' — two infinitives of what the custom is. 'purpureo… cothurno' — 'with a purple buskin' (the 'cothurnus' is the high hunting boot, also the actor's boot in tragedy). 'alte suras' — 'the calves high up'; 'alte' is an adverb. Tyre was known for its purple dye.

sentences.t: Punica regna vides, Tyrios et Agenoris urbem;
sentences.l: Punic kingdoms you see, Tyrians and Agenor's city;
sentences.i: What you see is a Punic realm, the Tyrians, and the city of Agenor;
sentences.n: 'Punica regna' — 'Punic' is the Latin form of 'Phoenician', as 'Poeni' above. 'Agenoris urbem' — 'Agenor's city': Agenor was an ancestor-king of Tyre in the Phoenician stories (the father of Cadmus and Europa). 'Tyrios' is the accusative plural, 'Tyrians', the same people as the 'Punica regna', since Carthage is a colony of Tyre. 'urbem' is the object of 'vides' with the other two.

sentences.t: sed fines Libyci, genus intractabile bello.
sentences.l: but the borders are Libyan, a race hard to handle in war.
sentences.i: but the country around is Libyan, a people not to be tamed in war.
sentences.n: 'sed fines Libyci' — 'but the territory (is) Libyan': 'est' omitted. 'genus intractabile bello' — 'a race (genus) not to be handled in war', in apposition to the people that 'fines Libyci' stands for; 'bello' is an ablative of respect, 'in war'. The Libyans (Gaetulians and Numidians) will matter later: Iarbas is the king who tries to marry Dido.

sentences.t:
Imperium Dido Tyria regit urbe profecta,
germanum fugiens.
sentences.l:
The rule Dido, from the Tyrian city having set out, holds,
her brother fleeing.
sentences.i: Dido, who came from the Tyrian city, holds the rule, fleeing her brother.
sentences.n: 'Imperium Dido… regit' — 'Dido holds the command'; 'Imperium' is first for emphasis, and the name is dropped in with 'Dido' only now. 'Tyria… urbe profecta' — 'having set out from the Tyrian city' ('profecta' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'proficiscor'; 'urbe' is ablative of separation, without 'ex'). 'germanum fugiens' — 'fleeing from her brother': 'fugio' takes a direct object. A 'germanus' is a full brother, who will be named in 347.

sentences.t:
Longa est iniuria, longae
ambages;
sentences.l:
Long is the injury, long
the windings;
sentences.i: The wrong is a long one, long the tangle of it;
sentences.n: 'iniuria' — 'wrong, injustice' (the second 'i' is consonantal, as in 'coniunx' in 343: iu is one syllable beginning with a y-sound). 'ambages' — 'going-round, winding paths', hence a roundabout story, a complicated tale; the word is feminine plural and the 'est' is carried over to it from 'longa est'. The adjectives 'longa… longae' repeat and frame the sentence.

sentences.t: sed summa sequar fastigia rerum.
sentences.l: but the chief heights I will follow of the matter.
sentences.i: but I will follow only the main heads of the story.
sentences.n: 'summa sequar fastigia rerum' — 'I shall follow the topmost points of the story', as if she were walking along the ridge of a roof and not through the valleys. 'fastigium' is a gable, a summit, hence a main point. 'rerum' — genitive of 'res', 'of the matter, of the events'. Venus declares she will skip to the highlights.

sentences.t:
Huic coniunx Sychaeus erat, ditissimus agri
Phoenicum, et magno miserae dilectus amore,
sentences.l:
To her a husband was Sychaeus, richest in land
of the Phoenicians, and by great love of the wretched one beloved,
sentences.i: Her husband was Sychaeus, the wealthiest landowner among the Phoenicians, and loved by the unhappy woman with a great love,
sentences.n: 'Huic coniunx Sychaeus erat' — 'to her there was a husband, Sychaeus' (dative of possession, with 'erat'). 'coniunx' — the 'i' is consonantal, so the word scans con | iunx. 'ditissimus agri Phoenicum' — 'richest of the Phoenicians in land' ('agri' is a genitive of respect; 'Phoenicum' is the ordinary third-declension genitive plural of 'Phoenices'). 'miserae' — 'the wretched one', the dative of agent with the participle 'dilectus': 'loved by the unhappy one'; 'miserae' foreshadows what happens to her later in the poem. 'magno… amore' — ablative of manner. This unit ends on a comma because the sentence goes on into the next unit; it is cut here to keep one clause to a tap.

sentences.t:
cui pater intactam dederat, primisque iugarat
ominibus.
sentences.l:
to whom her father had given her untouched, and had joined them with first
auspices.
sentences.i: to whom her father had given her as a virgin, and had united them under first auspices.
sentences.n: 'cui pater intactam dederat' — 'to whom her father had given her untouched', i.e. a virgin. 'primisque iugarat ominibus' — 'iugarat' is the contracted pluperfect of 'iugo', 'to yoke' (marry), 'iugaverat'; 'primis… ominibus' — 'with the first omens': a Roman marriage was begun under auspices, and 'primis' probably means that this was her first marriage, which makes her later situation heavier.

sentences.t:
Sed regna Tyri germanus habebat
Pygmalion, scelere ante alios immanior omnes.
sentences.l:
But the kingdoms of Tyre her brother held,
Pygmalion, in crime before all others more monstrous.
sentences.i: But her brother Pygmalion held the throne of Tyre, a man worse in crime than all other men.
sentences.n: 'Sed' — the turn to the villain. 'regna Tyri' — 'the kingdoms of Tyre', 'Tyri' is the genitive of 'Tyrus'. 'Pygmalion' — here a king of Tyre and brother of Dido, not the sculptor of Ovid, Metamorphoses 10; the name is a Phoenician name in Greek dress. 'scelere ante alios immanior omnes' — 'more monstrous in crime than all others': 'scelere' is ablative of respect, 'immanior' a comparative, and 'ante alios… omnes' ('before all the others', accusative plural) says what he is compared with, with the force of a superlative.

sentences.t: Quos inter medius venit furor.
sentences.l: Between them came a mad fury, in the middle.
sentences.i: Between them, in the midst, there came a savage rage.
sentences.n: 'Quos inter' — 'between whom': the preposition comes after the relative, as it often does in verse, and 'quos' is a connecting relative, 'between these two', Pygmalion and Sychaeus (the brother-in-law and the husband). 'medius… furor' — 'medius' agrees with the subject: 'madness came (as a thing) in the middle', i.e. it came between the two men; the 'furor' is Pygmalion's greed, which turns on Sychaeus.

sentences.t:
Ille Sychaeum
impius ante aras, atque auri caecus amore,
clam ferro incautum superat, securus amorum
germanae;
sentences.l:
That man Sychaeus
impious before the altars, and blind with love of gold,
secretly with iron overcomes the unwary, careless of the love
of his sister;
sentences.i: That godless man, before the altars and blind with love of gold, cuts Sychaeus down in secret with a blade, off his guard, caring nothing for his sister's love;
sentences.n: 'Ille Sychaeum… superat' — 'that man overcame Sychaeus': the subject, the object and the verb are held far apart by the line breaks and the phrases in between, an elegant hyperbaton: the victim's name stands at the end of its line, away from its verb. 'impius ante aras' — 'impious', because the murder is done at the altar, where a guest or kinsman is sacred, and Pygmalion is the opposite of Aeneas, 'pius'. 'auri caecus amore' — 'blind with love of gold'. 'clam ferro incautum superat' — 'overpowers, kills, the unaware man by the sword' (the 'ferrum', iron, is the weapon). 'securus amorum germanae' — 'free of care of his sister's loves': 'securus' takes the genitive; 'amorum' is plural, 'her love (for her husband)'. 'germanae' is a genitive.

sentences.t:
factumque diu celavit, et aegram,
multa malus simulans, vana spe lusit amantem.
sentences.l:
and the deed for long he concealed, and the sick one,
much an evil man pretending, with a vain hope he mocked, her loving.
sentences.i: and for a long while he hid what he had done, and, wicked and full of pretences, mocked with an empty hope the sick-hearted woman who loved.
sentences.n: 'factumque… celavit' — 'and he hid the deed' ('celo' here takes just the deed as its object). 'aegram… amantem' — both accusatives agree with an understood 'eam' (Dido), the object of 'lusit': 'her, sick at heart, loving'. 'multa malus simulans' — 'pretending many things', with a play on the 'm' sounds ('multa malus'). 'vana spe lusit' — 'he mocked with an empty hope': 'ludo' with an accusative object here, and 'spe' ablative of means. The brother lets her hope that her husband is still alive or will return.

sentences.t:
Ipsa sed in somnis inhumati venit imago
coniugis, ora modis attollens pallida miris,
sentences.l:
But herself in dreams came the image of the unburied
husband, lifting up a face pale in wondrous ways,
sentences.i: But in her sleep there came the very ghost of her unburied husband, raising a face pale in strange ways,
sentences.n: 'Ipsa sed' — 'sed' is postponed, 'but herself'; 'ipsa' stresses the appearance, the very image. 'in somnis' — 'in dreams' (Greenough's 'somnis' for 'somniis'). 'inhumati… coniugis' — 'of the unburied husband': the dead man has not had rites, so his ghost walks; 'imago' is a ghost or a dream-figure. 'ora… pallida' — 'ora' is plural for the one face (a poetic plural). 'modis… miris' — 'in wondrous ways', ablative of manner. This unit ends on a comma because the sentence goes on into the next unit, to 'retexit'.

sentences.t:
crudeles aras traiectaque pectora ferro
nudavit, caecumque domus scelus omne retexit.
sentences.l:
the cruel altars and the pierced breast by iron
he laid bare, and the blind crime of the house all unveiled.
sentences.i: he bared the cruel altar and his chest run through with iron, and laid open every secret of the crime done within the house.
sentences.n: 'crudeles aras traiectaque pectora ferro nudavit' — 'he laid bare the cruel altars and the breasts pierced through with iron' ('pectora' — plural for the one chest; 'traiecta' — the 'i' is consonantal, as after a prefix: tra-iecta). 'caecum… scelus' — 'the blind, hidden crime': 'caecus' here means 'unseen, dark', as opposed to its sense in 349 ('blind with love of gold'). 'retexit' — 'unwove, unravelled, uncovered'. The ghost shows the wound in the breast, and tells the truth of the crime.

sentences.t:
Tum celerare fugam patriaque excedere suadet,
auxiliumque viae veteres tellure recludit
thesauros, ignotum argenti pondus et auri.
sentences.l:
Then to hasten flight and from the fatherland to leave he urges,
and as help for the way the old, from the earth, he lays open
treasures, an unknown weight of silver and of gold.
sentences.i: Then he bids her hurry her flight and quit her country, and, to help her on the road, opens long-buried treasure in the earth, a store of silver and gold that nobody knew of.
sentences.n: 'suadet' — 'he urges': the subject is the ghost, 'imago'. 'celerare fugam patriaque excedere' — two infinitives after 'suadet' (one construction, 'persuade to do'); 'patria' is ablative of separation with 'excedere'. 'auxilium viae' — 'help for the journey', in apposition to 'thesauros'. 'veteres… thesauros' — 'thesauros' is a Greek word, accusative plural; Greenough gives 'veteres' in the accusative plural (-es). 'tellure' — ablative of place. 'ignotum… pondus' — 'an unknown weight', in apposition again, and the unknown is the reason the brother had not found it.

sentences.t: His commota fugam Dido sociosque parabat:
sentences.l: Moved by these things, Dido flight and companions prepared:
sentences.i: Stirred by this, Dido made ready her flight and her followers:
sentences.n: 'His commota' — 'moved by these things' (ablative of cause, with 'commota', the perfect participle). 'fugam sociosque parabat' — 'was preparing flight and companions': a 'zeugma', one verb that fits only one of its objects well ('prepare flight', 'make ready allies' in a stretched sense). The imperfect 'parabat' is the process, and the colon introduces what happened.

sentences.t:
conveniunt, quibus aut odium crudele tyranni
aut metus acer erat;
sentences.l:
gather, those to whom either hatred cruel of the tyrant
or fear sharp was;
sentences.i: they gather, all those who felt either bitter hatred of the tyrant or sharp fear;
sentences.n: 'conveniunt' — 'they come together'; the subject is not named, it is 'those who…' (the next relative clause stands for the subject). 'quibus… erat' — 'to whom there was' (dative of possession: 'to whom was hatred'). 'odium crudele tyranni aut metus acer' — 'tyrannus' is the Greek word for a ruler who has taken power outside the law, and Virgil uses it for Pygmalion; the adjectives 'crudele' and 'acer' pair the hatred and the fear.

sentences.t:
navis, quae forte paratae,
corripiunt, onerantque auro:
sentences.l:
ships, which by chance were ready,
they seize, and load with gold:
sentences.i: they seize ships that happened to be ready, and load them with gold:
sentences.n: 'navis' — Greenough's -is for the accusative plural ('naves'). 'quae forte paratae' — 'which by chance (were) ready': the verb 'erant' is dropped, an ellipsis of 'sunt/erant' with a participle. 'corripiunt' — 'snatch up'. 'onerant auro' — 'load with gold', the ablative of means. The colon opens the line that follows, which explains the cargo.

sentences.t:
portantur avari
Pygmalionis opes pelago;
sentences.l:
are carried the greedy
Pygmalion's riches over the sea;
sentences.i: the wealth of greedy Pygmalion is carried over the sea;
sentences.n: 'portantur… opes' — 'the resources are carried', plural 'opes', wealth. 'avari Pygmalionis' — 'avarus' is 'greedy for gain', here placed before the king's name, and the line break between them is neat: the greed of the man is the very treasure carried off. 'pelago' — 'over the sea' (ablative of the way). The irony is that his own gold, which he killed for, is stolen by her.

sentences.t: dux femina facti.
sentences.l: the leader of the deed a woman.
sentences.i: a woman is the leader of the deed.
sentences.n: 'dux femina facti' — 'leader of the deed, a woman': 'facti' is a genitive depending on 'dux'. The line has no verb at all, which gives it a short and weighty close. Venus gives Dido the praise of leadership before anything else.

sentences.t:
Devenere locos, ubi nunc ingentia cernis
moenia surgentemque novae Karthaginis arcem,
sentences.l:
They came to the places, where now huge you see
walls and the rising citadel of new Karthago,
sentences.i: They came to the place where now you see mighty walls and the rising citadel of the new Karthago,
sentences.n: 'Devenere' — 'devenerunt', 'they arrived' (the '-ere' for '-erunt' form, as in the pilot). 'locos' — an accusative of the place to which, 'to the places', without a preposition (plural 'loca/locos' is common). 'ubi nunc… cernis' — 'where now you see'; Venus speaks as if the city is already before them. 'surgentem… arcem' — 'the rising citadel', the Byrsa, which is actually the citadel of Carthage. 'novae Karthaginis' — the same words as in 298. This unit ends on a comma because the sentence goes on into the next unit, to 'tergo'.

sentences.t:
mercatique solum, facti de nomine Byrsam,
taurino quantum possent circumdare tergo.
sentences.l:
and bought the ground, from the name of the deed Byrsa,
so much as they could surround with the hide of a bull.
sentences.i: and bought a piece of ground—Byrsa, named from what was done—as much as one bull's hide would go round.
sentences.n: 'mercati' — the perfect participle of the deponent 'mercor', 'having bought'. 'facti de nomine Byrsam' — 'Byrsa, from the name of the deed': the name comes from Greek 'byrsa', 'hide' (Virgil does not say so, and his readers knew it). The story is that the Libyan king offered as much land as an ox-hide would cover; Dido cut the hide into very thin strips and encircled a hill. 'quantum possent circumdare' — 'as much as they could surround': the subjunctive 'possent' reports the terms of the bargain (as though in indirect speech). 'taurino… tergo' — 'with a bull's back', i.e. the hide. 'solum' is the ground.

sentences.t:
Sed vos qui tandem, quibus aut venistis ab oris,
quove tenetis iter?
sentences.l:
But you who at last, or from what shores have you come,
or whither hold your course?”
sentences.i: But who are you, in the end, and from what shores have you come, or where are you steering?”
sentences.n: The end of Venus's speech: she turns the questions on them. 'Sed vos qui tandem' — 'but you, who at last (are you)?' ('tandem' is 'at last, pray'). 'quibus aut venistis ab oris' — 'from what shores have you come': 'quibus' agrees with 'oris'; the 'ab' is placed after 'quibus aut'. 'quove tenetis iter' — 'or whither do you hold your way': 'teneo iter' means 'keep to a course'; '-ve' is 'or'. In Greenough's text the closing speech mark is printed with a space before it and none after ('iter? ”Quaerenti'), so a cut after the mark would fall in the middle of a word: the unit stops at 'iter?', the mark is carried in `l` and `i` here, and in the edition it stands at the head of the next unit's `t`.

sentences.t:
”Quaerenti talibus ille
suspirans, imoque trahens a pectore vocem:
sentences.l:
To her asking such things he,
sighing, and from the depth of his chest drawing his voice:
sentences.i: To her question he, sighing and drawing his voice up from the bottom of his chest, replied:
sentences.n: The edition prints the closing mark of Venus's speech glued to 'Quaerenti', so it stands at the head of this unit's `t`. 'Quaerenti' — dative singular of a present participle, agreeing with an understood 'ei' ('to her, asking'); 'talibus' — 'with such words', the whole speech. 'ille' — Aeneas, 'that one'. The verb of the sentence is left out (you'll see this constantly): the colon leads into the speech, and the participles ('suspirans', 'trahens') carry the manner. 'imo… a pectore' — 'from the bottom of the chest' ('imus' is 'lowest, deepest').

sentences.t:
“O dea, si prima repetens ab origine pergam,
et vacet annalis nostrorum audire laborum,
ante diem clauso componat Vesper Olympo.
sentences.l:
“O goddess, if from the first beginning going back I should proceed,
and there were leisure for you to hear the annals of our labours,
before, the day, Olympus being shut, would Vesper lay to rest.
sentences.i: “Goddess, if I were to go back and trace it from the first beginning, and you had time to hear the chronicle of our hardships, the evening star would lay the day to rest and shut the sky before I finished.
sentences.n: Aeneas's speech begins. 'O dea' — 'O goddess': he is polite, though he does not yet know who she is. 'si… pergam… et vacet' — a future-less-vivid condition, 'if I should go on… and if there were leisure': present subjunctives in the 'if' clause, 'componat' (present subjunctive) in the main clause. 'annalis' — Greenough's -is for the accusative plural, 'the annals, the yearly record' (the object of 'audire'), with 'nostrorum… laborum' ('nostrorum' is the genitive plural of 'noster', 'of ours'; 'laborum' of 'labores'). 'ante diem clauso componat Vesper Olympo' — 'ante' is an adverb, 'sooner, before I could finish'; 'diem' is the object of 'componat', 'would lay the day to rest', 'put the day to bed'; 'clauso Olympo' is an ablative absolute, 'Olympus (the sky) being shut'. 'Vesper' is the evening star.

sentences.t:
Nos Troia antiqua, si vestras forte per auris
Troiae nomen iit, diversa per aequora vectos
forte sua Libycis tempestas adpulit oris.
sentences.l:
Us from ancient Troy, if by chance through your ears
the name of Troy has gone, over diverse seas carried,
by chance its own tempest drove to Libyan shores.
sentences.i: Us—from ancient Troy, if the name of Troy has by any chance gone through your ears—carried over seas far apart, the storm, as it happened, drove to the Libyan coast.
sentences.n: 'Nos' is the object, put first and far from its verb 'adpulit' (377). 'Troia antiqua' — 'from ancient Troy' (ablative of origin, with no preposition). 'si vestras forte per auris Troiae nomen iit' — 'if by chance through your ears the name of Troy has gone': 'auris' is Greenough's -is for -es (accusative plural of 'auris'); 'iit' is the perfect of 'eo', the short form of 'ivit'. 'diversa per aequora vectos' — 'carried over different seas', 'vectos' agrees with 'nos'. 'forte sua' — 'by chance, of its own accord': 'sua tempestas' is 'its own storm', a storm that came of itself and not at our bidding. 'adpulit' — 'drove (us) to', Greenough's 'adpulit' for the familiar 'appulit'.

sentences.t:
Sum pius Aeneas, raptos qui ex hoste Penates
classe veho mecum, fama super aethera notus.
sentences.l:
I am dutiful Aeneas, who the seized from the enemy household gods
in my fleet carry with me, by fame above the sky known.
sentences.i: I am Aeneas, the devoted, who carry in my fleet the household gods I rescued from the enemy, and whose fame is known beyond the sky.
sentences.n: 'Sum pius Aeneas' — the reader has been told this since line 305; here he says it himself, with the epithet 'pius' as part of the name: he is a man known for devotion to the gods, which makes this a weighty first-person introduction. 'raptos qui ex hoste Penates' — 'Penates' are the household gods of the home and state, which Aeneas saved from Troy (II.717); 'raptos' agrees with 'Penates', and 'qui' is the relative 'who': the verb is 'veho' (379). 'classe veho mecum' — 'I carry with me in my fleet'. 'fama super aethera notus' — 'known by fame above the heavens', an exaggeration which has a touch of pride and a touch of the bitterness of someone nobody here knows.

sentences.t: Italiam quaero patriam et genus ab Iove summo.
sentences.l: Italy I seek as my fatherland, and a race from Jove most high.
sentences.i: I am looking for Italy, my homeland, and a stock that comes from Jupiter on high.
sentences.n: 'Italiam quaero patriam' — 'I seek Italy as a homeland' ('patriam' in apposition or predicate). 'genus ab Iove summo' — 'a race from highest Jove': Aeneas's own ancestry, the Dardan stock descended from Jupiter through Dardanus, who came from Italy; Italy is therefore the ancestral homeland, and 'genus' is the second object of 'quaero'. A short and simple line, in the style of an introduction.

sentences.t:
Bis denis Phrygium conscendi navibus aequor,
matre dea monstrante viam, data fata secutus;
sentences.l:
With twice ten ships the Phrygian sea I climbed,
my mother a goddess showing the way, the given fates following;
sentences.i: With twenty ships I took to the Phrygian sea, my mother, a goddess, pointing out the way, and I followed the fates assigned me;
sentences.n: 'Bis denis' — 'twice ten', distributive, 'twenty' (the 'bini' form 'denis' = 'ten each'; Virgil often uses distributives for large round numbers). 'Phrygium… aequor' — 'the Phrygian sea', i.e. the sea off Troy; Phrygia is used for Troy's land (Trojans are Phrygians in Roman verse). 'conscendi' — 'I embarked on, climbed on to', a verb of boarding which makes the sea a thing climbed. 'matre dea monstrante viam' — an ablative absolute, 'my mother, a goddess, showing the way': he says to her face, without knowing it, that his mother is a goddess. 'data fata secutus' — 'having followed the fates given (to me)'.

sentences.t: vix septem convolsae undis Euroque supersunt.
sentences.l: scarcely seven, wrecked by the waves and by the East Wind, remain.
sentences.i: scarcely seven, smashed by the waves and the east wind, are left.
sentences.n: 'vix septem' — 'barely seven' (of the twenty). 'convolsae' — 'wrenched, shattered', Greenough's 'convolsae' for 'convulsae'. 'undis Euroque' — ablative of means, 'by the waves and by the East Wind' (Eurus; the 'Eu' is one long syllable in the verse, the Greek diphthong, as in 'Teucris'). 'supersunt' — 'are left over, survive', plural to agree with 'septem'.

sentences.t:
Ipse ignotus, egens, Libyae deserta peragro,
Europa atque Asia pulsus.
sentences.l:
I myself unknown, destitute, the deserts of Libya wander through,
from Europe and Asia driven out.”
sentences.i: I myself, unknown and in want, roam the empty lands of Libya, driven out from Europe and from Asia.”
sentences.n: 'Ipse' — 'I myself', in contrast to the fleet. 'ignotus, egens' — the two nominatives, 'unknown, destitute' (asyndeton). 'Libyae deserta' — 'the deserts of Libya' ('deserta' is a neuter plural participle used as a noun, 'abandoned places'). 'Europa atque Asia pulsus' — 'driven from Europe and Asia': ablative of separation, without 'ex', in verse; Troy lay in Asia and the Trojans lost their homes there, and Europe was the place where they tried to settle in the early voyage (Book 3). The closing speech mark of Aeneas's speech is printed in the edition glued to the next word, 'Nec', so it stands at the head of the next unit's `t`; it is carried in `l` and `i` here.

sentences.t:
”Nec plura querentem
passa Venus medio sic interfata dolore est:
sentences.l:
Nor more complaining him
allowed Venus, in the middle of his grief, thus to interrupt:
sentences.i: Venus did not let him go on with his complaints, but broke in on him in the midst of his grief and said:
sentences.n: The speech ends and the narrator resumes (the edition prints the closing mark at the head of this unit's `t`). 'Nec plura querentem passa Venus' — 'Venus not having allowed him, complaining, (to say) more' ('passa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'patior', 'having allowed', with 'querentem' as its object; 'plura' is the neuter plural 'more things'). 'medio… dolore' — 'in the middle of his grief' (ablative). 'interfata est' — the perfect of the deponent 'interfor', 'to speak in the middle, interrupt', with a colon leading into Venus's speech in the next part (aeneid-005).
